title: 11/24/2026 | Harold Green | PC | Public comments opposing Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s request for good cause exemption relating to batch zero eligibility deadlines

=== PUC  59142 Opposition Letter.pdf ===
Before the Public Utility Commission of Texas
Project No. 59142
Review of ERCOT’s Interconnection Processes for Large Loads

Public Comments Opposing Synergen Green Energy, Inc.’s Request for a Good Cause
Exception Relating to Batch Zero Eligibility Deadlines

Dear Commissioners:

I am a resident of rural Calhoun County, living near the area where Synergen proposes its green
ammonia facility. I submit these comments in opposition to Synergen’s request (filed September
11, 2026) for a good cause exception that would let its approximately 300 MW project into
ERCOT’s Batch Zero process despite missing the July 10 and July 24, 2026 eligibility deadlines
set by PGRR 145.

Synergen and its supporters have circulated talking points claiming the company is a small-
medium developer that was unaware of the new rules, had no prior ERCOT experience,
reasonably relied on its transmission service provider, has already spent about $30.5 million, is
not a data center so should not be “collateral damage” to computational loads, will bring jobs and
tax revenue to a rural county, and will reduce grid strain through behind-the-meter solar and a
wind virtual power purchase agreement. Those points do not establish good cause, and they do
not justify special treatment.

Lack of awareness and lack of experience are not good cause

A company pursuing a project involving hundreds of millions of dollars and roughly 300 MW of
demand has a basic responsibility to track the regulatory process that governs interconnection.
Large-load reforms have been publicly discussed for some time amid the surge in
interconnection requests. PGRR 145 moved quickly after approval, but that does not excuse a
developer that has been working on this project since at least mid-2024 (when it first engaged
South Texas Electric Cooperative) from monitoring applicable rules. Claiming “we were
generally unaware” or “we had no prior experience” simply describes ordinary business risk. It is
not a legal or equitable basis for an exception under 16 TAC § 25.3(b). Reliance on the
cooperative is likewise not a substitute for the applicant’s own diligence. The cooperative does
not stand in the applicant’s shoes for meeting eligibility deadlines and financial security
requirements.

Money already spent does not satisfy or replace the financial security requirement

Synergen points to roughly $30.5 million already spent on permitting, engineering, assessments,
and site work, and notes that the security deposit would have been about $15 million.
Development spending and a security deposit serve different purposes. The security requirement
exists to help distinguish serious, ready projects from speculative ones and to protect the process
and other parties. Prior expenditures—especially before Final Investment Decision—do not
automatically prove readiness or entitle a project to skip a rule designed for that purpose.
Synergen’s further request to delay posting security until after the load study and Final
Investment Decision would effectively let it proceed through Batch Zero before meeting a core
eligibility filter. That is preferential treatment, not compliance.

 Being an industrial load does not create an automatic exception

The Batch Zero process and eligibility rules apply to large loads generally. Synergen emphasizes
that its project is green ammonia production rather than a data center and argues that industrial
loads should not be collateral to the wave of large computational loads. Different development
timelines are real, but the rules do not create a separate track or automatic waiver for industrial
manufacturing loads. Both types of load place demands on the transmission system and require
orderly study and commitment. Granting an exception because a project is industrial would
undermine the uniform process the Commission and ERCOT adopted to manage the overall
surge. The Commission should apply the same eligibility and security standards to all large-load
applicants.

Projected jobs and tax revenue do not override the rules, and the local picture is more
limited than the talking points suggest

Synergen cites roughly 60 permanent jobs, peak construction employment, and total
expenditures around $568 million, along with expansion of the local tax base for Calhoun
County, the school district, the groundwater conservation district, and the port. Those figures are
projections, not guarantees. Even if realized, approximately 60 permanent jobs for a 300 MW
facility is a modest number relative to the scale of the load and the special treatment requested.
Moreover, Synergen has sought a Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETT) taxable-value
limitation for the school district. Any abatement reduces the school-tax benefit that supporters
highlight. Broader economic activity claims should be weighed against real local concerns that
residents have raised for months: brackish groundwater withdrawals from the same aquifer
system that serves nearby homes, farms, and ranches; potential discharge impacts on bays; land-
use changes in a rural residential and agricultural area; and the cumulative effect of large
industrial projects on water resources and community character. The site is frequently described
in ways that can obscure its true rural location near the Calhoun/Jackson County line (Olivia/Port
Alto area) rather than the industrial core of Point Comfort. Accelerating grid access for a project
whose local benefits are limited, partly abated, and contested does not create good cause.

Claims of “green” power do not eliminate the need for the standard large-load process

Synergen states it will pair the load with roughly 290. MW of behind-the-meter solar and about
600 MW of Texas-sourced wind through a virtual power purchase agreement, and that this aligns
with approaches that can reduce net transmission burden. Green ammonia production via
electrolysis is inherently electricity-intensive. Even with co-located renewables, the project still
requires approximately 300 MW of firm grid capacity. Behind-the-meter solar is intermittent. A
virtual power purchase agreement is a financial arrangement, not firm, local, dispatchable
generation. These features do not convert a large firm load into something that can bypass
eligibility deadlines or financial security. The project still requires grid interconnection, studies,
and capacity. Labeling the project “green” does not exempt it from the front-end rules that apply
to every other large-load applicant. These attributes may be relevant later in system studies; they
are not a reason to waive the eligibility framework designed to manage the overall surge in large
loads.

Prior project experience does not support special treatment

 Synergen previously advanced a similar green ammonia project in Hamilton County, Nebraska.
That proposal encountered significant local opposition, particularly over water use and related
infrastructure concerns. In 2024 the local planning process did not endorse the project, and
Synergen ultimately paused development and withdrew its conditional-use permit application.
While the company has continued to list a Nebraska project in its pipeline, the experience
illustrates that advancing these facilities is not always straightforward and that prior development
spending does not automatically demonstrate readiness or justify exceptions from established
eligibility rules. The Texas project should be held to the same standards that apply to other large-
load applicants.

Compressed timelines and precedent

I recognize that PGRR 145 took effect on a short schedule after approval. That fact deserves
consideration in general process design. It does not, however, create good cause for an individual
applicant that has been developing a major load for more than a year and that failed to meet
published deadlines. If the Commission begins granting exceptions based on claimed
unawareness, lack of prior experience, reliance on a cooperative, or money already spent on
development, the eligibility framework loses its force. Other applicants will make similar
arguments. Consistent application protects the integrity of the process and treats all large loads
the same.

Request

For these reasons, I respectfully ask the Commission to:
¢ Deny Synergen’s request for a good cause exception from the Batch Zero eligibility
deadlines.

¢ Require full compliance with the same eligibility and financial security rules that apply to
other large-load applicants.

¢ Require documentation supporting any claimed investments, readiness, and financing
rather than accepting those assertions at face value.

° Avoid creating a precedent that allows applicants to miss deadlines and obtain special
treatment on the basis of unawareness, reliance on third parties, or prior development
spending.

An applicant’s investment claims, projected economic benefits, or the financial consequences of
missing a deadline do not, by themselves, establish good cause. The rules exist for a reason.
Please apply them uniformly and deny the requested exception.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Harold Gfeen
President

Port Alto HOA District 1 Water System
